content: The use of safety-engineered syringes has been generally perceived as user-friendly, safe, and well-tolerated by patients. Reports of technical issues with these devices have been minimal. However, studies have shown inconsistent preferences and satisfaction levels among nurses. The studies reviewed also had methodological limitations. The panel expressed uncertainty regarding the cost-effectiveness of introducing sharps injury protection (SIP) devices, as this aspect was not covered in the systematic reviews. A subsequent cost-effectiveness study conducted by the SDS Department demonstrated preliminary evidence supporting the cost-effectiveness of these devices, with the results expected to be published soon and considered in future guideline updates. It is anticipated that market forces, such as economies of scale and competition, will reduce unit prices, further improving the cost-effectiveness of SIP devices. There is a notable lack of published research from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). For example, an unpublished PATH study on retractable syringes in South Africa was noted but excluded from the review due to its unpublished status. The use of SIP devices is considered a critical component of a comprehensive approach to injection safety. The estimated costs of implementing these recommendations should account for all components of this comprehensive strategy, including the cost of the devices themselves. The WHO guideline recommends the use of syringes with a re-use prevention (RUP) feature for HCWs administering intramuscular, subcutaneous, or intradermal injectable medications. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. While peer-reviewed studies directly linking RUP syringes to reduced re-use are lacking, evidence from immunization programs using auto-disable (AD) syringes strongly suggests that the benefits outweigh the risks and are likely to reduce re-use. A pending WHO cost-effectiveness study supports this recommendation. In settings where RUP devices have been introduced, post-intervention assessments have documented a decrease in syringe re-use rates, leading to a reduction in diseases transmitted through unsafe injection practices. No significant harms are expected, and greater benefits are anticipated in regions with higher disease prevalence and syringe re-use rates. The values and preferences of HCWs regarding these devices depend heavily on their cultural and professional background, as well as awareness campaigns highlighting the risks of injury and disease transmission. A systematic review of attitudes and feasibility identified evidence from six studies indicating that safety syringes are generally perceived as easy to use, safe, and well-tolerated by patients. However, nurses’ preferences and satisfaction varied across studies, and the included studies had methodological limitations. The WHO guideline emphasizes the need for further research on the harms, benefits, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness of adopting RUP and SIP devices for intramuscular, subcutaneous, and intradermal injections. Specific research needs include effectiveness studies in LMICs, disease burden studies related to syringe re-use and NSIs, and cost-effectiveness analyses. Additionally, better integration of RUP and SIP features into a single device by manufacturers is recommended. The guideline also highlights the importance of addressing waste management and the environmental impact of new devices. Adequate provision of safety boxes for the safe collection of used devices is essential. Post-marketing surveillance is needed to monitor defects, effectiveness, and any issues encountered during the use of these devices. Monitoring and evaluation plans with appropriate indicators should be established to assess the adoption, adaptation, and impact of the guideline globally. Injection safety assessments, clinical audits, supervision, and NSI reporting systems are some of the tools suggested for monitoring implementation. The WHO strongly recommends that all countries transition to the exclusive use of safety-engineered injection devices, such as RUP and SIP syringes, by 2020, where appropriate. This transition should be supported by national policies and based on local epidemiological data on syringe re-use and NSI rates. WHO will assist countries with high burdens of bloodborne diseases and unsafe injection practices in gathering local data to facilitate this transition. Finally, the guideline will be reviewed and updated as new evidence becomes available. WHO encourages suggestions for additional questions to be evaluated during future reviews. The ultimate goal of this guideline is to improve the quality and safety of care and health outcomes related to injection practices. Dissemination, adaptation, and implementation of the guideline are critical steps to achieve this goal.
